blocks.title: Modeling
blocks.body:
The modeling stage is where data becomes intelligence - and where the ethical properties of the AI system begin to take shape. Choices made here, such as which features to include, how to weight different outcomes, and what to optimise for, all carry ethical consequences.

This is also the stage where bias can emerge or be amplified, and where the tools of responsible AI - explainability, documentation and security testing - are most directly applied.

blocks.title: If you use AI tools rather than build them
blocks.body: You won't be testing a model's performance across demographic groups or writing its model card - the vendor should have done that already. But knowing these are the checks a responsible developer runs turns them into fair questions you can ask: does this tool have a model card? Has its performance been tested across the groups it's actually used with? That's a reasonable thing to ask of any AI vendor - including the one your own organisation already uses.

blocks.title: The frameworks suggest...
blocks.body:
The EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to achieve appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity - and to be sufficiently transparent that deployers can understand and oversee their operation.

ISO 42001 recommends that AI systems be evaluated against defined performance criteria, with documentation of known limitations and risks - including records that allow the system's behaviour to be explained and audited, before and after deployment.

items.title: Why explainability matters
items.body: When an AI system makes or influences a decision that affects a person - whether they receive a loan, a job interview, or a medical diagnosis - that person has a legitimate interest in understanding why. Explainability is not just a technical goal; it is an ethical and legal requirement.
items.graphicAlt: A magnifying glass inspecting a document, representing scrutinising a decision

items.title: Types of explainability
items.body: Global explainability helps us understand how the model behaves overall - which features it weighs most heavily. Local explainability helps us understand why the model made a specific decision in a specific case. Both matter for responsible AI, serving different stakeholders.
items.graphicAlt: A large outlined circle (the overall model) containing a smaller solid circle (one specific decision)

items.title: Explainable AI (XAI) tools
items.body: Tools such as LIME, SHAP and counterfactual explanations are designed to make AI reasoning interpretable to humans. They translate complex model outputs into language that can be understood, challenged and acted upon - by developers, decision-makers and those affected.
items.graphicAlt: A cog, representing the tools used to inspect how a model works

items.title: Ask yourself
items.body:
• Could you explain to someone why your AI made the decision it did about them?
  • Are there groups for whom the AI's reasoning is less well understood?
  • What would you do if an AI decision appeared wrong or unfair?
items.graphicAlt: A question mark in a circle

items.title: Testing for bias
items.body: Before deployment, AI models should be tested not only for overall accuracy but for differential performance across groups. A model that is 90% accurate overall may be significantly less accurate for minority groups - a pattern that must be detected and addressed before the model goes live.

items.title: Model cards
items.body: Model cards are structured documents describing an AI model's intended use, performance across demographic groups, known limitations and ethical considerations. Originally proposed by Google researchers, they are now a widely adopted best practice for transparent AI documentation.

items.title: AI security testing
items.body: AI systems face specific security risks: adversarial attacks (inputs designed to fool the model), data poisoning (corrupting training data) and model inversion (extracting personal data from a trained model). Security testing is an important and often overlooked component of responsible development.

items.title: Generative AI and LLM-specific risks
items.body: Generative AI and large language models (LLMs) introduce risks that don't map neatly onto the security concerns above. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - an industry-standard reference, updated as new risks emerge - currently ranks prompt injection (getting a model to follow hidden or disguised instructions instead of its intended ones) as the single most significant LLM risk, followed by sensitive information disclosure (a model revealing training data, or another user's data, in its responses) and excessive agency - an AI agent taking actions beyond what it was actually authorised to do, exactly what happened in the case study covered later in this course. The same list names misinformation - a model confidently generating false information (often called 'hallucination') that then drives flawed decisions - as a named risk in its own right, not just a quality quirk to shrug off. See the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications for the current full list.

items.title: Environmental impact
items.body: Training and running large AI models consumes significant energy and water for data centre cooling, and contributes to electronic waste from specialised hardware. Independent estimates put the training of OpenAI's GPT-3 alone at around 552 tonnes of CO2 equivalent; larger, more capable models are estimated to run considerably higher, though AI companies rarely disclose exact figures - itself a transparency gap. The EU's Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI and UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI both name environmental sustainability as a core requirement of ethical AI, not a side effect to overlook - a model's environmental footprint is a legitimate factor to weigh against its benefits, alongside more familiar concerns like accuracy and fairness.

items.title: Implementation tips
items.body:
• Test performance separately for different demographic groups - not just overall accuracy.
  • Produce a model card documenting limitations and ethical considerations before deployment.
  • Include security testing as a standard part of your development process, not an afterthought.
  • Set a threshold for acceptable differential performance - and don't deploy until it's met.
  • Weigh a model's compute, energy and environmental footprint against its benefits - and prefer a smaller or more efficient model when it meets the need just as well.

blocks.title: Case study: Facial recognition and bias
blocks.body:
A 2018 study by MIT researcher Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru examined commercial facial recognition systems from IBM, Microsoft and Face++. All three systems performed significantly worse on darker-skinned faces - and worst of all on darker-skinned women, with error rates up to 34 percentage points higher than for lighter-skinned men.

The systems had been trained predominantly on images of lighter-skinned individuals, reflecting the demographics of the datasets used. The bias was not a programming error - it was a direct consequence of unrepresentative training data and a failure to test for differential performance before deployment.

blocks.title: Case study: Facial recognition and bias
blocks.instruction: Select one option, then select Submit.

items.text: Using a more advanced modeling algorithm with higher overall accuracy.
Collecting significantly more training images overall.
Testing the model's performance separately across demographic groups, rather than overall accuracy alone.
Using synthetic training data instead of real images.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The bias was detectable through disaggregated testing - breaking down performance metrics by demographic group. Testing for overall accuracy alone would have missed the problem. Responsible AI requires differential testing across the groups a model will be applied to, before deployment.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. The bias was detectable through disaggregated testing - breaking down performance by demographic group. Overall accuracy alone would have missed it. This is why responsible AI requires differential testing across all groups a model will be applied to.

blocks.title: Coming up...
blocks.body: Once an AI system is built and tested, the work of responsible AI enters a new phase. In Deployment and Beyond, we'll look at monitoring AI systems in the real world, governing their use, and ensuring accountability over time.
